segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, while a promise of entering his rest still remains, let us be afraid that any one of you should be found to have fallen short of it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we too have had good news proclaimed to us, just as they did; but the word they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united in faith with those who listened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we who have believed are entering that rest, just as he has said,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “As I swore in my anger, ‘They shall never enter my rest,’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: even though his works were finished from the foundation of the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For somewhere he has spoken about the seventh day in this way:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and again in this passage:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “They shall never enter my rest.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since, then, it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly had the good news proclaimed to them did not enter because of disobedience,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he again appoints a certain day, “Today,” saying through David after so long a time, in the words already quoted,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken afterward about another day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the one who has entered God’s rest has also rested from his own works, just as God did from his.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let us therefore make every effort to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by following the same example of disobedience.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing as far as the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And no creature is hidden from his sight, but everything is naked and laid bare to the eyes of the one to whom we must give account.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since, then, we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast to our confession.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tested in every way just as we are, yet without sin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let us then approach the throne of grace with boldness, so that we may receive mercy and find grace for help at the right time.

notes.note: The Greek verb can mean 'seem' or 'think', or 'be judged, be found'. The rendering takes it in the last sense, as a warning about an actual verdict. Others read it as a softened expression ('should seem to have fallen short') or as 'should think he has come too late' for the promise.

notes.phrase: they were not united in faith with those who listened
notes.traditional: not being mixed with faith in them that heard it
notes.note: The manuscripts differ by one letter. The reading translated here, which has the stronger manuscript support, says that the wilderness generation was not joined in faith to those who truly listened. The other reading says the word itself was not combined with faith in its hearers, and older English versions follow it. The general point is the same on either reading.

notes.phrase: They shall never enter my rest
notes.traditional: They shall not enter my rest
notes.note: The Greek literally reads 'If they shall enter my rest', reproducing a Hebrew oath formula in which the penalty clause is left unspoken ('may such-and-such happen if...'). It functions as an emphatic denial. The quotation is from Psalm 95 in its Greek form, already cited in the previous chapter.

In Greek the names Joshua and Jesus are identical. The context, leading Israel into the land, shows that Joshua son of Nun is meant, but a Greek reader would have heard the shared name, and the author may intend the contrast between the first Joshua and Jesus.

The author here switches from the word for 'rest' used throughout the chapter to a different and rare word meaning Sabbath observance, not attested in surviving Greek before this passage. It ties the promised rest to God's own rest on the seventh day, cited in verse 4.

Most interpreters take this as a general statement about any believer who enters God's rest. A minority read it as referring specifically to Christ, who has finished his work and entered that rest ahead of his people. The Greek allows either.

The verb is formed from the word for 'neck' and its exact image here is uncertain. Suggestions include a wrestler gripping an opponent's neck or the bending back of a sacrificial victim's neck to expose the throat. The general sense of being exposed and defenceless is not in doubt.

notes.phrase: to whom we must give account
notes.traditional: with whom we have to do
notes.note: The Greek is terse: literally 'toward whom for us the word'. It can mean 'to whom we must render account' or more loosely 'with whom we have to deal'. The word translated 'account' is the same one translated 'word' in verse 12, so the passage opens and closes with the same term.

The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that this translation keeps wherever God's dwelling is in view. Many English versions also keep the plural in this verse, though some flatten it to 'heaven'.

The Greek verb covers both testing and tempting; English must choose. 'Tested' is used here because the surrounding argument concerns Israel's testing in the wilderness and endurance under trial, and several modern versions do the same. 'Tempted' remains the more common rendering and is not wrong, since the trial includes the pull toward sin, as 'yet without sin' implies.

candidates.reason: English must choose between 'test' and 'tempt' in dozens of passages across the Gospels, Paul, Hebrews and James, and inconsistent choices would hide the links between them.
Recurs in John, Acts, Paul and Hebrews with renderings ranging over 'boldness', 'confidence', 'openness' and 'frank speech'; a governing decision would keep these aligned.
With its verb ἀπειθέω it wavers in translations between 'disobedience' and 'unbelief', which matters for how Hebrews, Romans and John relate faith and obedience.
Very frequent verb rendered variously as 'preach the gospel', 'bring good news' or 'evangelize'; needs one policy coordinated with the noun εὐαγγέλιον.
The 'rest' vocabulary of Hebrews 3–4 overlaps in English with ἀνάπαυσις (Matthew 11:29) and σαββατισμός; a decision is needed on whether and how to distinguish them.
